scenario: AITA got refusing to back up for someone who drove the wrong way up to an ATM? | My bank has kind of an odd set up for their ATM out front. It’s in a small cut out with clearly marked arrows pointing to which way the entrance is, in addition to the fact that since this is a drive up ATM it makes sense for the machine to be on the left side where the driver would be sitting. That said, it’s very easy for people to turn I to the outcropping the wrong way. This happened today while I went to get some cash. I arrived at my bank and as I took the turn to go into the ATM cut out, another car whipped into it going the wrong way so that their passenger could use the ATM. I was annoyed at this as I was just about to pull up to it and I was in kind of a hurry, since I needed to get to class. She took 15 minutes to do her transactions. She went through at least 3 cards inserting and reinserting the cards at least 2 times each. I sat patiently, yet annoyed, and waited for her to finish. But when she was done was reaching my limit of patience, she then leant out the window of her car and yell at me to move, I didn’t respond, no one was waiting behind me, I had already been late to class, so being more late wouldn’t kill me. I didn’t move. After about 5 minutes of her shouting at me to move, she backed up did a K-turn and left. I told my friend about this when I eventually arrived at class and he told me that I was being a dick for not just backing up since there was no one behind me. However I stick to the notion that I was in the right for not moving because they were going against traffic. AITA?

Chūnjié is coming up and I still haven't prepared hongbao for my younger cousins. How would you handle that?

No worries! Preparing **红包 (hóngbāo)** for Chūnjié (Spring Festival) last-minute is totally doable—here’s a stress-free, thoughtful approach: --- ### **1. Quick & Practical Hongbao Ideas** **A. Cash Hongbao (Traditional & Safe)** - **Amount:** Follow local customs (e.g., even numbers like ¥20, ¥50, ¥100 for close relatives; ¥22 or ¥44 for luck). Avoid odd numbers or ¥4 (sounds like "death" in Mandarin). - **Packaging:** - **Red envelopes (红包袋):** Buy pre-made ones at supermarkets (e.g., Walmart, Costco) or online (Taobao, Amazon). Look for **gold/red foil** for extra festivity. - **DIY:** Use red paper (available at craft stores) + glue/stickers. Add a **gold seal (印章)** or calligraphy for a personal touch. - **Alternative:** Use **red envelopes with QR codes** (e.g., WeChat Pay/Alipay) for digital hongbao (if your cousins are tech-savvy). **B. Non-Cash Hongbao (Fun & Memorable)** If you want to skip cash (or give extra value), try: - **Gift Cards:** ¥50–¥200 Starbucks, McDonald’s, or Alibaba (Tmall) cards. Kids love these! - **Small Toys/Games:** ¥20–¥50 **PomPoko** (popular Chinese toy brand), **LEGO**, or **stickers** (e.g., Disney, Hello Kitty). - **Food Coupons:** Vouchers for their favorite snacks (e.g., "¥30 for a box of Mooncakes" or "¥50 for a meal at [local restaurant]"). - **Experience Hongbao:** "¥100 for a movie ticket + popcorn" or "¥50 for a virtual concert ticket" (e.g., Bilibili or Tencent Music). - **Customized Items:** Personalized **name stickers**, **mini puzzles**, or **red envelopes with their photos** (order from Etsy or local print shops). **C. Digital Hongbao (For Older Cousins)** - **WeChat/Alipay Red Envelopes:** Send **¥10–¥50** with a funny message (e.g., "For your future success! 🎉"). Add a **GIF** or **sticker** to make it special. - **Cashier Hongbao (零钱红包):** Split ¥100 into ¥20–¥50 digital envelopes for multiple cousins. --- ### **2. Last-Minute Tips** - **Buy in Bulk:** Supermarkets (e.g., Carrefour, H Mart) or **Taobao** often have red envelopes in packs. Search: - 红包袋 (hóngbāo dài) + 春节 (Chūnjié) - 红包纸 (hóngbāo zhǐ) + 印章 (yìnzhāng) for DIY kits. - **Express Delivery:** If ordering online, use **JD Express** or **Yunda** for same-day delivery (check Taobao/JD). - **Wrap It Nice:** Add a **red ribbon**, **gold washi tape**, or a **handwritten note** (e.g., "祝你新年快乐！" *Zhù nǐ xīnnián kuàilè!* = Happy New Year!). - **Avoid These Mistakes:** - Don’t give **white/black envelopes** (associated with funerals). - Skip **odd amounts** (e.g., ¥15) or ¥4 (bad luck). - Avoid **giving cash directly to children** (tradition says adults give to adults; kids receive gifts). --- ### **3. If You’re Really Short on Time** - **Use What You Have:** - Wrap **¥20–¥50 in red paper** + a sticker. - Give **a small toy + ¥10** (e.g., a keychain + cash). - **Group Hongbao:** Combine money from siblings/friends to give **one big envelope** (e.g., ¥200 total split among cousins). - **Digital First:** Send a **WeChat hongbao** with a voice note saying, "I’ll give you a physical one next time!" --- ### **4. Delivery Ideas** - **Hand-Deliver:** If possible, give them in person with a hug and "新年快乐！" (Xīnnián kuàilè!). - **Post It:** Use **China Post** (if they’re far) or **JD Courier** (fast and reliable). - **Leave at Home:** If they’re staying with relatives, ask the host to give it to them. --- ### **5. Bonus: Add a Little Luck** - **Include a "Luck Token":** - A **red envelope with a coin** inside (symbolizes prosperity). - A **small "福" (fú = luck) charm** or **mandarin orange** (symbolizes wealth). - A **handwritten fortune** (e.g., "This year, you’ll get an A+ in exams!"). --- ### **Example Checklist (1-Hour Prep)** | Task | Where to Get It | Cost (Approx.) | |--------------------|--------------------------|----------------| | Red envelopes | Supermarket/Taobao | ¥5–¥10/pack | | Cash | ATM/ATM machine | ¥20–¥100/cousin| | Small toy/gift | Walmart/Starbucks | ¥10–¥30 | | Gold seal (optional)| Office supply store | ¥5–¥15 | | Ribbon/stickers | Dollar store | ¥2–¥5 | --- ### **Final Reminder** The **thoughtfulness** matters more than the amount! Even a **handmade envelope with ¥20 and a smile** will make them happy. If you’re still unsure, **digital hongbao** is the safest bet. **祝你包红包顺利！** (Zhù nǐ bāo hóngbāo shùnlì! = Wish you smooth hongbao-giving!) prediction.raw: This is a nuanced situation that depends on **context, safety, and cultural norms**—especially in a **drive-thru ATM scenario**. Here’s my breakdown of why your friend might argue you were "being a dick" (1) and why you might still feel justified (0), along with a **balanced perspective**: --- ### **Why Your Friend Might Say "1 (AITA)"** 1. **Drive-Thru Etiquette Overrides "Wrong Way"** - Drive-thrus (even for ATMs) are designed for **one-way flow** to avoid collisions. The woman’s mistake was **not a traffic violation**—it was a **user error**, not a deliberate wrong-way drive. - **Real-world logic**: If you refuse to move, you create a **deadlock**. The woman couldn’t exit without backing up, and you couldn’t proceed without moving. This risks: - **Blocking the lane** (potential hazard for other drivers). - **Escalating aggression** (her yelling was likely stress-induced, not malicious). - **Wasting time** (you were already late; her 15-minute ATM session was her problem, not yours). 2. **The ATM’s Design is Ambiguous** - Your bank’s arrows might be **misleading** if they don’t clearly indicate a **one-way loop**. Many drive-thru ATMs assume: - You pull in, park, and exit the same way. - The "wrong way" might be **intuitive** for someone unfamiliar with the layout (e.g., tourists, elderly, or distracted drivers). - **Solution**: If this happens often, suggest the bank **adds a "No U-Turn" sign** or **reconfigures the ATM** to face the lane’s natural flow. 3. **Your Reaction Was Emotionally Charged** - You were **annoyed + late**, which clouded your judgment. Yelling back (even silently) could’ve escalated tension. - **Alternative**: A **polite but firm** approach (e.g., honking once + waving for her to exit) might’ve resolved it faster. --- ### **Why You Might Feel Justified (0)** 1. **"Wrong Way" is Technically Illegal** - In most places, **driving against traffic** (even in a dead-end ATM lane) is a **traffic violation**. While it’s rare to get ticketed for this, it’s still **reckless behavior**. - **Your right**: You had the **legal right to the lane**—she was occupying space she shouldn’t have been in. 2. **Safety First** - If she **hadn’t noticed you**, she could’ve backed into you. Your refusal to move was a **passive safety measure**. - **But**: This assumes she was *fully* unaware, which is unlikely in a drive-thru ATM (people usually check mirrors). 3. **Time Sensitivity** - You were **already late**, and her delay made you **more late**. While her actions were her responsibility, your **patience had limits**. --- ### **The Verdict: It’s a 0.5 (Neither Fully Right Nor Wrong)** This isn’t a **black-and-white** situation. Here’s how to split the blame: - **50% Your Friend’s Argument**: - You **could’ve moved** without risking a collision. Drive-thrus prioritize **flow over technical "wrongness."** - Your **annoyance + lateness** made you less patient than you should’ve been. - **50% Your Argument**: - She **violated basic traffic logic** by going the wrong way. - **Not moving wasn’t aggressive**—it was a **logical stand** in a poorly designed system. --- ### **How to Handle It Next Time (If It Happens Again)** 1. **Assume Good Intentions** - Most people don’t **intend** to drive wrong way—they’re distracted or confused. A **calm honk + wave** often works better than silence. 2. **Use Verbal Cues** - Say something like: *"Excuse me, ma’am, you’re facing the wrong way. Could you back up?"* - This is **polite but firm** and gives her a chance to correct herself. 3. **Document for the Bank** - If this is a **frequent issue**, email the bank: *"The ATM’s current layout causes confusion. Could you add a ‘No U-Turn’ sign or adjust the machine’s position?"* 4. **Prioritize Safety Over "Rightness"** - If someone is **truly stuck**, moving (even slightly) to let them exit is safer than a stalemate. --- ### **Cultural Context (China/US/EU)** - **China**: Drive-thru ATMs are **less common**, but if this happened, locals might **side with you**—wrong-way driving is seen as **rude**. However, **patience is valued** in traffic. - **US/EU**: Drive-thrus are **standard**, and **flow > technical rules**. Refusing to move would likely be seen as **stubborn**. --- ### **Final Thought** You weren’t *wrong* for not moving, but you **could’ve handled it better**. The **real issue** is the **ATM’s poor design**—if the bank fixed it, this wouldn’t keep happening. Next time, **assume the other driver is human (not malicious)**, and **prioritize de-escalation**. Would you like help drafting an email to the bank about the ATM layout?
